query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, a subtle transformation of the grain‐boundary complexion—specifically, the stress‐ and temperature‐induced emergence of short‐range ordered clusters at the grain boundaries—reduces grain boundary cohesion and triggers brittle behavior. This mechanism is distinct from conventional precipitation or extensive segregation because it involves a nanoscale complexion transition rather than the formation of continuous intermetallic phases.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy with uniformly disordered grain boundaries and high toughness.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simulated service conditions that combine moderate thermal aging (e.g., at temperatures on the order of 500–700°C for durations reflecting service exposure) with applied tensile loading to promote stress-assisted complexion transformation.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant thermal and mechanical conditions (moderate temperatures and strain rates) under which the alloy remains compositionally complex without overt phase separation; comparisons are made with conventional alloys subjected to analogous aging and loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of localized, nanoscale short-range ordered (SRO) clusters along grain boundaries which subtly alter the complexion from a ductile disordered state to a brittle, ordered state.
generation.mechanism: Under combined thermal and mechanical loading, the high configurational entropy initially keeps the grain boundaries chemically uniform. However, mechanical stresses coupled with modest thermal activation drive a redistribution of solute atoms that encourages SRO at the boundaries. This modified complexion reduces the ability of the boundaries to absorb deformation (by hindering dislocation emission and promoting intergranular decohesion), thereby leading to a decrease in toughness before any large-scale or overt precipitation occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Following the intervention, the HEA specimens will show a measurable reduction in fracture toughness and ductility. Atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM will detect the emergence of nanoscale SRO clusters at grain boundaries, a change that is absent in the as-cast state and is different in morphology from the conventional large-scale precipitates observed in standard alloys.
generation.baseline: An as-cast or solution‐treated single-phase HEA with homogeneous grain boundary chemistry and high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected under moderate thermal aging and typical service strain rates; at temperatures high enough to drive complete phase separation or at conditions with negligible thermal exposure, either conventional precipitation or no transformation, respectively, will dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The thermodynamic driving force and kinetics for the onset of grain-boundary SRO in these alloys are not fully quantified. It remains uncertain how sensitive the complexion transformation is to variations in temperature, stress magnitude, and alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens with identical initial single-phase microstructures and similar conventional alloy specimens as controls. Subject one set of HEA samples to combined thermal aging (500–700°C) and a controlled tensile load, while maintaining a second set under the same thermal conditions without applied load. Use comparable treatments for the conventional alloys known to develop grain-boundary precipitation. Characterize all samples before and after treatment using atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to assess grain boundary chemistry and structural state, alongside mechanical toughness tests (e.g., fracture toughness, impact testing).
measurements: Quantitative fracture toughness and ductility measurements
Grain boundary compositional profiles via APT
Direct imaging of grain-boundary complexion states (e.g., presence of SRO clusters) via TEM
Nanoindentation of grain boundary regions to assess local cohesive strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA specimens do not develop detectable short-range ordering or a modified grain-boundary complexion (i.e., no nanoscale SRO clusters) after the combined thermal and mechanical treatment, or if any drop in toughness correlates solely with conventional large-scale precipitate formation similar to that seen in conventional alloys, then the hypothesis that a complexion transformation drives brittleness is falsified.
